name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 16 December 1967

clue.text: Aspiring young musicians?

blocks.note: surface reading: an ambitious youth orchestra or pop group
setter's reading: a group named for hope, the Victorian temperance society for children

explanation.surface: Talented teenagers dream of making it big with their music.
explanation.walkthrough: The Band of Hope was a British temperance organisation for children, founded in 1847; its 'band' is a group, not musicians, and 'aspiring' is its hope.
explanation.definitionFit: The society's members were young people pledged to abstinence, gathered together in hopeful fellowship rather than playing instruments.

clue.text: An important order for washers

blocks.note: first meaning: a senior British order of knighthood
second meaning: the tub that people washing themselves sit in

explanation.surface: A hardware supplier lands a large contract for washers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Order of the Bath is a British order of chivalry; washers here are people who wash themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a prestigious chivalric order and the tub that people who wash themselves sit in.

clue.text: Butter for the nursery?

blocks.note: surface reading: dairy spread for the children's room
setter's reading: a butter is an animal that butts, and the nursery suggests a nanny

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the children's room needs its own supply of butter.
explanation.definitionFit: A female goat butts with its head, and its common name contains the word for a children's nurse.

clue.text: O, it's a place in Italy

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken together

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims on recognising an Italian place.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal: the setter trusts the solver to notice that the opening words hold exactly the letters of the town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostia is the ancient port of Rome at the mouth of the Tiber, still a coastal town in Italy.

clue.text: It's easy to spoil the Greek soldiers

indicators.note: easy suggests something loose and relaxed, so the letters that follow may slacken out of their order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken together

explanation.surface: A warning that some Greek soldiers could easily be spoilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoil' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'easy' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoplites were the heavily armed infantrymen of the ancient Greek city states, fighting in a phalanx.

clue.text: The man at the wheel perhaps

definitions.text: The man at the wheel perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: The man at the wheel perhaps
blocks.note: surface reading: a driver steering a car

blocks.clueFragment: The man at the wheel perhaps
blocks.note: setter's reading: a craftsman shaping clay on a spinning wheel

explanation.surface: The driver steering the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceramic craftsman throws clay pots while seated at a rotating wheel, so he too is a man at the wheel.

clue.text: In perfect shape for cricket

blocks.note: surface reading: a player fully fit for the cricket season
setter's reading: a geometric shape that is also a famous cricket ground

explanation.surface: A cricketer is in top condition for the coming match.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a Test cricket ground in south London, and cricket fields are typically egg-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: The egg-like figure is the shape of most cricket fields, and also the name of the famous London ground.

clue.text: A member of the Ladies' String Orchestra?

definitions.text: A member of the Ladies' String Orchestra?

blocks.clueFragment: A member of the Ladies' String Orchestra?
blocks.note: surface reading: one woman who plays in an all-female string ensemble

blocks.clueFragment: A member of the Ladies' String Orchestra?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a string instrument that is also a woman's name

explanation.surface: A player in an all-women string orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: Viola is a girl's name, best known from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: The alto instrument of the violin family belongs in any string section, and shares its name with a woman.

clue.text: One in the habit of singing as he works?

definitions.text: One in the habit of singing as he works?

blocks.clueFragment: One in the habit of singing as he works?
blocks.note: surface reading: a cheerful worker who always sings on the job

blocks.clueFragment: One in the habit of singing as he works?
blocks.note: setter's reading: habit is a monk's robe and a lay is a song

explanation.surface: A cheerful labourer who habitually sings while working.
explanation.walkthrough: A lay is an old word for a song; a habit is the robe of a religious order.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay brother is a monastery member who does manual work rather than holy orders, robed in a habit.

clue.text: He used to have the whiphand

definitions.text: He used to have the whiphand

blocks.clueFragment: He used to have the whiphand
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who once held the upper hand

blocks.clueFragment: He used to have the whiphand
blocks.note: setter's reading: a driver of former times who literally held the whip in his hand

explanation.surface: A man who was once in control but has lost his power.
explanation.definitionFit: The driver of a horse-drawn carriage held the reins and whip, a job largely gone since motor cars.

clue.text: The principle's the same, anyway

indicators.note: a word that is the same whichever way it is read runs identically forwards and backwards

blocks.note: the definition alone; the rest of the clue says the word reads identically from either end

explanation.surface: Someone insists the underlying principle is unchanged regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyway' here means 'whichever way you read it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a belief or doctrine held as true, which is what a principle is.

clue.text: Science of some use to the Gibraltarian?

definitions.text: Science of some use to the Gibraltarian?

blocks.clueFragment: Science of some use to the Gibraltarian?
blocks.note: surface reading: a branch of learning helpful to people living in Gibraltar

blocks.clueFragment: Science of some use to the Gibraltarian?
blocks.note: setter's reading: Gibraltar is known as the Rock, so its people live on a rock

explanation.surface: A field of study that might help the residents of Gibraltar.
explanation.walkthrough: Gibraltar, the British territory at the tip of Spain, is nicknamed the Rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrology is the scientific study of rocks, their origin and composition, apt for those living on the Rock.

clue.text: It may provide many with diet — and a good blowout!

indicators.note: to provide is to make up or produce, so these letters may be made into something new

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A meal plan that feeds the masses and ends with a big feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowout' looks like a slap-up meal, matching the diet; here it is an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamite is a high explosive, and a blowout is a violent bursting apart, so a good one needs plenty.

clue.text: Furniture with a hundred locks

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: A piece of furniture fitted with a hundred locks, like a strongbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests security fittings, but they are locks of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat for one person with a back is a basic item of household furniture.

clue.text: A doubtful condition

blocks.note: surface reading: an illness or state of health whose diagnosis is uncertain
setter's reading: a state of mind full of doubt

explanation.surface: A medical condition about which the doctors are unsure.
explanation.definitionFit: Scepticism is the attitude of questioning and distrusting claims, a mental state defined by doubt.

clue.text: He is in a fitting occupation

definitions.text: He is in a fitting occupation

blocks.clueFragment: He is in a fitting occupation
blocks.note: surface reading: a man whose job suits him well

blocks.clueFragment: He is in a fitting occupation
blocks.note: setter's reading: a man whose trade involves fitting customers with garments

explanation.surface: A man has found a job that suits him.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothier makes or sells garments, and fitting customers for suits is central to that trade.

clue.text: Would it make a woman hot-headed?

definitions.text: Would it make a woman hot-headed?

blocks.clueFragment: Would it make a woman hot-headed?
blocks.note: surface reading: something that might make a woman quick-tempered

blocks.clueFragment: Would it make a woman hot-headed?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a hairdo set with heat would literally warm her head

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what would make a woman lose her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as a hairdresser's heat-set wave, though it means a spell of very hot weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell of sweltering weather would leave anyone's head hot, and a heat-set hair wave would too.

clue.text: A stubborn creature has most of the charm

blocks.clueFragment: A stubborn creature has most of the charm
blocks.note: surface reading: an obstinate animal is nonetheless rather charming

blocks.clueFragment: A stubborn creature has most of the charm
blocks.note: setter's reading: the words for one obstinate beast spell all but the last letter of a lucky charm

explanation.surface: A stubborn animal turns out to be mostly charming.
explanation.walkthrough: A MULE is the stubborn creature; add T and it becomes the answer, so the mule is most of the charm.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a small ornament worn as a charm to ward off evil or bring luck.

clue.text: Be quick, or you may be late!

blocks.clueFragment: Be quick, or you may be late!
blocks.note: surface reading: hurry up or you will miss the start

blocks.clueFragment: Be quick, or you may be late!
blocks.note: setter's reading: quick is the old word for living and late means dead

explanation.surface: A parent hurrying a dawdling child out the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The quick and the dead' uses quick to mean living; 'the late Mr X' means the deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an order to hurry and be alert, which is what 'be quick' commands.

clue.text: Glasses for Jack and Jill

blocks.note: first meaning: flat-bottomed drinking glasses
second meaning: the nursery-rhyme pair who fell down the hill

explanation.surface: Choosing drinking glasses for a couple called Jack and Jill.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Jack fell down and Jill came tumbling after, so both are fallers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a straight-sided drinking vessel and those who fall head over heels, as the rhyme's pair do.

clue.text: Snooker-player called to the bar?

blocks.note: surface reading: a snooker player who becomes a barrister
setter's reading: someone who sinks balls, working behind a pub counter

explanation.surface: A snooker professional qualifies as a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Called to the bar' means admitted as a barrister; a potman is a pub worker who collects glasses and serves.
explanation.definitionFit: A snooker player pots balls, and a potman is an assistant in a public house who handles the pint pots.

clue.text: Fish-frying instruction in the garden

definitions.note: a phrase locating the answer rather than a noun; it points to a garden plant

blocks.note: first meaning: split in two, an order to flip the flatfish in the pan
second meaning: a plant whose flowers follow the sun, grown in gardens

explanation.surface: Someone gives cooking directions for frying fish at a garden barbecue.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as an instruction, it tells you to flip the sole in the pan; as one word it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Turnsole is an old name for plants such as heliotrope whose flowers turn towards the sun, grown in gardens.

clue.text: Firm turntables

indicators.note: turning things about upsets their arrangement, so the letters right after it get rearranged

blocks.note: the word after the four-letter signal at the front of this compound, taken as written

explanation.surface: A company that makes record-player turntables.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word 'turntables' hides both the signal and the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm and stable are synonyms meaning steady, secure and not likely to move or collapse.

clue.text: How an only child may become a brother?

definitions.text: How an only child may become a brother?

blocks.clueFragment: How an only child may become a brother?
blocks.note: surface reading: a puzzle about gaining a sibling without parents having more children

blocks.clueFragment: How an only child may become a brother?
blocks.note: setter's reading: through marriage, by a legal tie rather than blood

explanation.surface: A riddle about how someone with no siblings could be a brother.
explanation.walkthrough: Marrying someone with siblings makes an only child a brother-in-law.
explanation.definitionFit: Relatives by marriage are related through law rather than birth, so a spouse's sibling gains a legal brother.

clue.text: A Sharp answer

blocks.note: surface reading: a curt or witty reply from someone
setter's reading: a sour fruit, as in the old saying that the answer's one

explanation.surface: Someone gives a cutting retort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The answer's a lemon' is an old British saying for an unsatisfactory reply or a flat no; the fruit is also sharp-tasting.
explanation.definitionFit: The citrus fruit tastes tart, and in the British idiom an evasive or useless reply is called one.

clue.text: Got no bag for winter sports

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken together

explanation.surface: Someone has arrived at a ski resort without luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal; the solver must spot that the opening words hold exactly the right letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A toboggan is a long sledge ridden down snowy slopes, one of the classic pastimes on snow and ice.

clue.text: Lizard, not in Cornwall

blocks.note: surface reading: a rocky headland located somewhere other than Cornwall
setter's reading: a reptile, rather than the place name

explanation.surface: A place called Lizard found outside Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lizard is a peninsula in Cornwall, England's south-western county; this lizard is the animal instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Geckos are small tropical reptiles with sticky toe pads, a lizard found far from Cornish shores.

clue.text: Drinks shunned by the doctor

definitions.note: an ink pad or blotter drinks up inks, so the clue leans on the word for both roles

indicators.note: something shunned is avoided and kept out, so the following letters are left out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
DR is the standard abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor refuses to touch alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: With no separate definition, the clue relies on the result being a real word: writing fluids.
explanation.definitionFit: Inks are liquids for writing or printing, which blotting paper soaks up, a loose sense of drinks.

clue.text: Not exactly what is mean by being in a fix

definitions.text: Not exactly what is mean by being in a fix

blocks.clueFragment: Not exactly what is mean by being in a fix
blocks.note: surface reading: being in a fix does not quite mean being in trouble

blocks.clueFragment: Not exactly what is mean by being in a fix
blocks.note: setter's reading: something fixed in place, literally stuck fast

explanation.surface: Someone quibbles over what being in a fix really means.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is printed as 'mean' for 'meant'. Taken literally, being fixed means unable to move, though the idiom means being in difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Something firmly fixed cannot be shifted, so it cannot be moved at all, the literal sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Memorial for the "Terriers"?

definitions.note: plural, while the answer is one breed name

blocks.note: first meaning: a heap of stones raised as a monument
second meaning: a breed of small Scottish terrier

explanation.surface: A monument raised to honour a unit nicknamed the Terriers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army soldiers were nicknamed Terriers; the cairn terrier is a Scottish dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cairn is a heap of stones piled up as a landmark or monument, and gives its name to a terrier breed.

clue.text: It's not so bad, being on this

definitions.text: It's not so bad, being on this

blocks.clueFragment: It's not so bad, being on this
blocks.note: surface reading: something that is fine to stand or sit on

blocks.clueFragment: It's not so bad, being on this
blocks.note: setter's reading: the idiom for recovering from illness, being on the up

explanation.surface: Someone reassures you that a situation isn't too bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the mend' means getting better after illness, so things are no longer so bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone recovering from sickness is said to be on the improve, so their condition is getting less serious.

clue.text: They get paid for late duty

definitions.text: They get paid for late duty

blocks.clueFragment: They get paid for late duty
blocks.note: surface reading: workers paid extra for a night shift

blocks.clueFragment: They get paid for late duty
blocks.note: setter's reading: retired people drawing money for work done in years gone by

explanation.surface: Night-shift workers receive extra pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means former here, not after hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired people receive regular payments in return for their years of past service at work.
